Brazil’s government is taking a victory lap because the IACHR freedom of expression rapporteur issued a report that mentions Brazil has functioning institutions. 

Congratulations—your country has a Constitution and a Supreme Court. But an IACHR country review is not a gold medal. It’s what happens when serious concerns have escalated enough that the Commission sends a rapporteur to evaluate risks to free expression and due process.

The IACHR is the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights of the OAS. Its Special Rapporteur for Freedom of Expression exists to monitor and alert when member states start normalizing “exceptional” restrictions on speech and political participation. A rapporteur doesn’t fly in because everything is fine. He flies in because there are warning signs that need to be confronted while there’s still time to reverse course.

And that’s exactly what the report does. It does not “certify” Brazil as a model. It repeatedly warns about the dangers of vague standards and open-ended emergency logic. 

In the section on online speech, the report lays out three core concerns: transparency, notification to affected users, and due process around the restriction of content/accounts (see pp. 54–60; esp. paras. 134–148).

The report also addresses how orders are issued to platforms, how much reasoning is provided, whether platforms can participate, and whether users are told why they’re being restricted (paras. 140–143). One of the most serious points is the insistence that judicial restrictions must be fully reasoned and must satisfy legality, necessity, and proportionality (para. 144). That is the opposite of “trust us.”

The report then rejects the idea that “online moderation” can become a loophole for state censorship-by-proxy. It stresses that restrictions like blocking platforms/domains are extreme measures, and references international standards (including the Manila Principles) that call for specificity, transparency, and procedural safeguards (paras. 146–148). In essence, it reprimands Brazil for blurring the line between “platform policy” and “state order” to avoid accountability.

So watching the Brazilian government applaud itself for being audited is… something. It’s like a company celebrating that it’s being audited. The point of the IACHR process is to force clarity where power has been exercised using elastic labels like “disinformation” as a regulatory weapon rather than a defined legal category.

For Rumble and Trump Media, this matters because our case is about the same underlying problem the rapporteur is flagging, the use of coercive state power to force platforms to suppress speech, including speech that is lawful where it is posted, and to do it through procedures that are opaque, accelerated, and difficult to challenge.

The IACHR report is not a pat on the back. It’s a fire alarm wrapped in diplomatic language. Brazil should treat it like a roadmap back to normal democratic standards.

Full report is available at https://t.co/St9bP6gxgJ
